findings.location: Section 3, 'The identity and notification bars' — 'no Linux agent implements the round-trip anywhere'; repeated in Section 6 'Notifications, end to end' — 'Actionable notifications have no Linux implementation anywhere'
findings.finding: The draft asserts a flat absence that the vault's own evidence contradicts. halinuxcompanion — a Linux agent — implements the actionable-notification round-trip: its README advertises 'Actionable Notifications (Triggers event in Home Assistant)' and 'Notification cleared/dismissed (Triggers event in Home Assistant)' via a local aiohttp HTTP server that HA POSTs to. The draft cites this very project two paragraphs earlier (for its 'Move sensors to MQTT' concession) while claiming the round-trip has 'no Linux implementation anywhere'. The claim is load-bearing: it is what lets the draft conclude 'MQTT-only sacrifices almost nothing the ecosystem delivers'.
findings.evidence: [[github-muniterhalinuxcompanion-homeassistant-linux-companion-github]] — README Features: 'Actionable Notifications (Triggers event in Home Assistant)', 'Notification cleared/dismissed (Triggers event in Home Assistant)', 'HTTP Server (aiohttp): Listen to POST notification service call from Home Assistant' (with the honest caveat that its To-do lists 'Finish notifications functionality'). [[interim-report-adopt-vs-build-honest-verdict]] says it plainly: 'halinuxcompanion implements mobile_app with an HTTP server for the notify round-trip but is a 90-star Python project that itself lists "Move sensors to MQTT"'.
findings.suggested_fix: In Section 3, replace 'no Linux agent implements the round-trip anywhere' with a scoped claim: the round-trip exists on Linux only in the native-API class — halinuxcompanion implements it over mobile_app with a local HTTP server (a 90-star Python project whose own to-do wants to move sensors to MQTT because the native API strands values offline) — while no MQTT-transport agent implements it (go-hass-agent #667/#926 maintainer-silent, lnxlink one-way). Apply the same correction in Section 6. Note: the corrected claim is actually STRONGER for the thesis — the only Linux round-trip implementation lives in a project that concedes MQTT is the better transport — so the fix sharpens rather than weakens the argument.

findings.location: Section 4A — 'the launcher mutual-exclusion select is one bash module away, because the mutual exclusion already lives in the systemd units and polkit rules'; echoed in 4B — '"One bash module away" carries a heavy deployment cost'
findings.finding: The steel-man's sharpest sentence misstates lnxlink's extension surface: per lnxlink's own docs, the bash-command module creates 'custom sensors, binary_sensors, buttons, or switches using shell scripts' — it cannot emit a select entity at all. The draft never lands this direct hit, and worse, it understates the adopter's real move: custom modules CAN host dropdown-shaped entities (the Lutris Game Launcher dropdown ships as a custom module, and the Steam launcher dropdown is first-class), so the honest strongest form is 'one custom module away', which is stronger for the adopter than the bash-module form the draft gives and then refutes.
findings.evidence: [[lnxlink]] — Bash Commands module: 'Create custom sensors, binary_sensors, buttons, or switches using shell scripts' (no selects); Custom Modules table: 'Lutris Game Launcher — Discussion #202'; Steam module: 'Launch Steam or non-Steam games from a dropdown list' (first-class).
findings.suggested_fix: Correct the mechanics in two moves. In 4B, add the direct refutation the vault supplies: even the concession as stated is too generous — lnxlink's bash surface cannot emit selects, so the launcher select is not 'one bash module away' but 'one custom module away'. Then acknowledge the Lutris-dropdown precedent as the adopter's genuine path (a custom module CAN host a game-launcher select) and answer it on the remaining ground: the mutual-exclusion semantics, the state round-trip through the shared state topic reflecting real systemd unit state, and the declarative generation from jupiter.services.haAgent.launcherApps have no module precedent — lnxlink modules are hand-written per host, not generated from fleet configuration.

findings.location: Section 4A, end of the steel-man ('The maintenance arithmetic clinches it...') and Section 4B 'Second, the expressibility record' — the fork between the two is missing
findings.finding: The adopt-vs-build interim names the adopter's honest path explicitly — 'contribute a NixOS module + launcher-exclusion select upstream (go-hass-agent takes feature requests; the audio-select gap shows its control vocabulary CAN be extended), or wrap lnxlink' — and the draft drops the first half entirely. Its steel-man covers 'adopt as-is and glue' and 'wrap lnxlink', but never 'extend the incumbent upstream', which is the move that dissolves the expressibility objection over time and is the strongest form of the counter-position. The refutation's ingredients exist on the page (zero-occurrence changelog through v14.15.1; #667/#926 open with zero maintainer engagement) but are never assembled against the named fork.
findings.evidence: [[interim-report-adopt-vs-build-honest-verdict]] — Position A closing: 'The honest adopter's path: contribute a NixOS module + launcher-exclusion select upstream (go-hass-agent takes feature requests; the audio-select gap shows its control vocabulary CAN be extended), or wrap lnxlink.' Same note: go-hass-agent issues #667 (Dec 2025) and #926 (Aug 2026) open with no maintainer reply.
findings.suggested_fix: In 4B (either in the packaging counter or as a short third prong before 'the expressibility record'), name the fork and answer it in 2-3 sentences: the obvious adopter's rebuttal is to PR select support and a NixOS service module upstream rather than glue around the gaps — but the evidence on record says that path runs through a maintainer whose changelog shows zero select/state-sync occurrences across 3,909 commits and whose two open notification feature requests have sat unassigned since December 2025, so contributing upstream means paying the solo-maintainer wait on someone else's release cadence, which is the same maintenance arithmetic the objection itself raises, with less control.

findings.location: Section 6 — 'Mesh/exit-node health (callisto, fleet visibility)' — 'an unverified backend maps onto the host where the mesh hub runs'
findings.finding: The draft places the mesh hub on callisto; the vault's ground truth places headscale on europa, and the draft's own Section 1 does too ('europa runs nothing despite the zfs/syncthing/headscale backends existing for exactly that host'). The privilege-ladder interim's host audit reads 'The server set is europa (ZFS NAS + iscsi target + syncthing + headscale + harmonia)' while callisto runs a headscale *target* (a tailnet client) — an internal contradiction (Section 1 vs Section 6) that misattributes the backend-headscale gap.
findings.evidence: [[interim-report-headless-privilege-ladder]] — 'The server set is europa (ZFS NAS + iscsi target + syncthing + headscale + harmonia) and callisto (iSCSI-root compute + broker + postgres + tunnel host)'; callisto's inventory lists 'headscale-target' with '(europa)' marking the syncthing hub. [[interim-report-adopt-vs-build-honest-verdict]] — 'europa (ZFS NAS + headscale server + syncthing) doesn't run it despite backend-zfs/backend-syncthing/backend-headscale existing for exactly that host'.
findings.suggested_fix: Retitle the Section 6 gap to 'Mesh/exit-node health (europa, fleet visibility)' and correct the body: the unverified backend-headscale maps onto europa, the host where the mesh hub runs; callisto's agents would report peer/exit-node state as tailnet members. This also restores consistency with Section 1's own claim.

findings.location: Section 4B, 'The packaging counter first' — 'its Python dependency surface — pygobject3, ewmh, xlib, opencv-python, pulsectl, pyalsaaudio, docker, speechrecognition in one propagated list — is why a 2025 packaging attempt failed'
findings.finding: The draft misattributes causation to its cited evidence: the 2025 packaging attempt failed on a setuptools version pin ('ERROR Missing dependencies: setuptools~=68.0.0, wheel~=0.40.0'), not on the GUI/audio dependency surface — and the first forum reply hands over the one-line postPatch fix. An adopter reading the citation will object that the 'failure' was a trivial version-pinning issue solved in the thread's first response. The load-bearing fact (lnxlink has no nixpkgs package and no one has upstreamed a service module — an unmerged draft exists from Aug 2024) survives untouched, but the causal gloss distorts the source.
findings.evidence: [[python-packaging-error-needs-specific-setuptools-version-nixos-discourse]] — the error is 'Missing dependencies: setuptools~=68.0.0, wheel~=0.40.0'; the reply: 'you need to relax the version requirements for setuptools: postPatch = substituteInPlace pyproject.toml --replace-fail "setuptools~=68.0.0" "setuptools"'. The note also carries the real module-absence evidence: an unmerged 'Ensure the Python package is installed when lnxlink is enabled' draft (GitHub issue #334089, Aug 2024).
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite the causal claim in that sentence: the packaging attempt shows the friction is real (an individual hit a wall in Oct 2025 and no module has been upstreamed in the year since the Aug 2024 draft), and the dependency surface is the ongoing per-release maintenance cost for whoever owns the packaging — rather than claiming the surface caused that particular failure. Keeps the refutation honest and immune to the one-line-fix rebuttal.

findings.location: Lead paragraph — 'the symptom is live right now: all four TCxWave kiosks read UNAVAILABLE on callisto's Home Assistant instance at this moment [[interim-report-mqtt-lifecycle-supervisor-spec]]'; repeated in Section 1 — 'The four kiosks' entities read unavailable on callisto's HA right now'
findings.finding: The headline presenting symptom is attributed to the wrong source: the mqtt-lifecycle-supervisor-spec interim does not contain the live-fleet observation — its body covers the defect audit and supervisor spec. The live finding entered the corpus at the step-8 gap wave (the corpus critic's inherited live observation, binding via comparisons.md update 8), and no vault note carries it. Compounding this, 'at this moment' is a point-in-time observation written into a durable report — the claim goes stale the moment any kiosk reconnects, and it currently borrows the credibility of a defect-audit interim that never made the observation.
findings.evidence: research/runs/linux-agent-jupiteros-fleet-15537b/comparisons.md gap-wave update 8: 'Live presenting symptom: the four kiosks' HA entities read UNAVAILABLE on callisto's HA right now — the exact "never reliable" complaint, live. The audit section cites this as the presenting evidence'; research/runs/linux-agent-jupiteros-fleet-15537b/temp/corpus-critic-results.md: 'Live finding inherited (from the critic): The four kiosks' HA entities currently read UNAVAILABLE on callisto's HA'. A grep of the cited interim shows no live-observation claim.
findings.suggested_fix: In both the lead and Section 1, re-anchor the claim's provenance and date: attribute the observation to the run's live audit (2026-09-02, the step-8 gap wave) rather than to the supervisor-spec interim, and phrase it as dated rather than perpetual — e.g. 'the run's live audit on 2 September 2026 found all four kiosks reading UNAVAILABLE on callisto's HA'. Keep the [[interim-report-mqtt-lifecycle-supervisor-spec]] citation on the two-bugs diagnosis, where it belongs.

findings.location: Section 5C, SMART bullet — 'with the man-page caveat that "smartd will block until the executable PATH returns", so the hook is fire-and-forget'
findings.finding: The sentence contradicts itself: if smartd blocks until the hook executable returns, the hook cannot be fire-and-forget as written — the correct design consequence is the opposite: because smartd blocks, the hook itself must be a fast hand-off that publishes into the agent's channel and exits immediately (detached spawn or socket write), never an inline MQTT publish. As written, a reader implementing the design could write a blocking hook that stalls smartd's monitoring loop.
findings.evidence: [[smartdconf5-smartmontools-debian-testing-debian-manpages]] — '-M exec' blocking semantics; [[interim-report-headless-privilege-ladder]] — the hook 'hands it to the agent, which never touches the ioctl' (hand-off design, no inline-publish claim).
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite the clause to spell out the design rule: 'because smartd blocks until the hook returns, the hook must be a fast hand-off — write the SMARTD_* event to the agent's channel and exit immediately (a detached spawn or socket write), never an inline publish that would stall smartd's monitoring loop.'

findings.location: Section 4B — 'the unified identity stops not-working the moment the ConnAck supervisor lands, which is days of work, not a research programme'; Section 8 Phase 1 — 'the ConnAck supervisor (one to two weeks...)'
findings.finding: Internal inconsistency an adopter can exploit: the refutation of 'a split identity that works beats a unified identity that doesn't' rests on the fix being imminent ('days of work'), but the draft's own Phase 1 prices the same work at one to two weeks (including the regression tests, broker pairing, and backoff). The mismatch invites the reply that the report understates its own cure to win the argument.
findings.evidence: Draft-internal: Section 4B vs Section 8 Phase 1; [[interim-report-mqtt-lifecycle-supervisor-spec]] prices the supervisor as one structural change plus the D4-D9 spec items.
findings.suggested_fix: Align the two: either change 'days of work' to 'one to two weeks, per the Phase 1 estimate' in Section 4B, or scope the 'days' claim to the two core fixes only (ConnAck re-subscribe plus availability re-assert) with the full supervisor at one to two weeks.

findings.location: Section 4B — 'adopting means inheriting two devices per host, unsynchronised controls, an MQTT v5 broker requirement, and manual registration'
findings.finding: The MQTT v5 item is listed as an adoption cost, but the vault's own tension analysis establishes that callisto's mosquitto is version-current and v5 is available — the requirement costs approximately nothing on this fleet. Resting part of the refutation prong on a cost the fleet's broker already covers overstates the adopter's burden and hands the adopter an easy rebuttal ('your v5 point is void, our broker is current') that taints the neighbouring, load-bearing items (unsynced controls, split-brain, no service module).
findings.evidence: Source-tension 2 (research/runs/linux-agent-jupiteros-fleet-15537b/temp/source-tensions.json), side B: 'the fleet's mosquitto (callisto) is version-current — v5 is available'; resolution: 'go-hass-agent's v5 requirement is adoptable if the broker is upgraded' — i.e. a configuration detail, not a blocker.
findings.suggested_fix: Either drop 'an MQTT v5 broker requirement' from the cost list or qualify it in place ('an MQTT v5 requirement — already satisfied by callisto's version-current mosquitto, so a non-cost here'), letting the unsynced-controls and split-brain items carry the prong.

findings.location: Section 2A — 'Paho, the alternative, exposes rich reconnect callbacks but leaves re-subscription application-owned too, and drags a C toolchain onto every NixOS fleet build'
findings.finding: The fitness interim states the Paho cost with an explicit hedge the draft drops: the C objection is a dependency chain in every host closure, and the interim flags as an OPEN question whether nixpkgs already packages paho-c cleanly — 'If it's clean, the C-toolchain objection weakens'. If nixpkgs packages the C library, the fleet never touches the toolchain itself; the draft asserts the cost flatly without the interim's own caveat or the verification.
findings.evidence: [[interim-report-rumqttc-dependency-fitness]] — 'default builds need CMake + a C compiler + system OpenSSL, which in a jupiterOS (NixOS) fleet context means a foreign C dependency chain in every host closure'; its open question: 'Paho on NixOS: what does the paho-c + paho.mqtt.rust packaging story actually look like in nixpkgs today? If it's clean, the C-toolchain objection weakens (though the same-owned-resubscription fact still keeps rumqttc ahead for this codebase)'.
findings.suggested_fix: Add the hedge or the verification: either 'a foreign C dependency chain in every host closure (unless nixpkgs' paho-c packaging is already clean — unverified)' or run the nix eval check the interim prescribed and state the result. The application-owned re-subscription point alone decides the client question, so the hedge costs the argument nothing.

findings.location: Section 3, opening — 'The 2026 Linux field divides into companion-class candidates (go-hass-agent, lnxlink, halinuxcompanion) and monitoring-class stacks'
findings.finding: The field enumeration omits two Linux-capable candidates the vault's own alternatives table carries: System Bridge (Windows/Linux, HA API over WebSocket — the one non-MQTT, non-mobile_app Linux transport) and IoTuring (cross-platform, MQTT). System Bridge is the notable omission: as a WebSocket-API companion it is a third transport class that the 'want control and the ecosystem routes you to MQTT' resolution never names, though it inherits the same native-API concession (the halinuxcompanion stuck-sensors/offline problem) that the draft uses against the class.
findings.evidence: [[lnxlink]] — canonical alternatives table: 'System Bridge — Windows, Linux — HA API (WebSocket)'; 'IoTuring — Cross-platform (Windows, Linux, macOS, BSD) — MQTT'; also surfaced in [[wth-there-is-no-windows-and-linux-ha-app-similar-to-macos-month-of-what-the-heck]].
findings.suggested_fix: One sentence completing the enumeration and classing the omissions: System Bridge joins the native-API class and inherits the halinuxcompanion concession (values stranded when the host goes offline — no LWT); IoTuring is MQTT-transport with a thinner surface than lnxlink. Alternatively, state the cut explicitly ('System Bridge and IoTuring, named in the alternatives table, are excluded as WebSocket-API/thinner-MQTT variants covered by the class arguments').
